mcqs.question: What is the primary purpose of a take-home README, given that a reviewer wasn't present while you built the solution?
options: To restate what the code does, since the reviewer may not read the code itself
To list every library and version used, for compliance purposes
To narrate the reasoning and decisions the reviewer couldn't otherwise observe
To pad the submission so it looks more complete
mcqs.explanation: The README substitutes for the live narration you'd give in a synchronous interview — the why behind decisions, not just a restatement of what the code visibly does (which the reviewer can see by reading it). Listing dependencies has a place but isn't the primary purpose, and padding is the opposite of what's valuable.

mcqs.question: Given a limited time budget, where should test-writing effort go first?
options: Evenly across every function, regardless of how risky or trivial each one is
Toward simple getters and mappers, since those are the fastest tests to write
Skipped entirely in favor of more features, since take-homes rarely check tests
Toward the riskiest logic and boundary conditions the code is least obviously correct on
mcqs.explanation: Limited test time is a prioritization exercise — spend it where a bug is least obvious and most consequential, not spread evenly or on trivial code that's obviously correct on a manual run. Take-homes commonly do check for tests, and skipping them is a missed signal.

mcqs.question: Which trade-offs section entry is the strongest signal to an evaluator?
options: "I'd add more tests and clean up the code with more time."
"I'd add tests for concurrent writes to the same record, since the current implementation doesn't handle that race."
"Everything is done; there's nothing I'd change."
"I ran out of time, sorry."
mcqs.explanation: A specific, technically precise gap shows real judgment and awareness of a concrete failure mode. A generic statement says nothing useful, claiming nothing is missing is rarely credible, and an unqualified apology gives the evaluator no information to work with.

mcqs.question: Why should you test your take-home's setup steps from a fresh clone right before submitting, rather than trusting your development machine?
options: Your development machine likely has stray global installs or cached state that masks a missing setup step
Fresh clones run faster than a machine with a lot of installed software
It's required by most take-home rubrics as a checklist item
It makes the git history look cleaner to the evaluator
mcqs.explanation: A dev machine accumulates global tools, cached dependencies, and environment variables set weeks ago — any of which can silently make a broken setup process look fine to you while it fails for a reviewer starting from nothing. Speed and git history aren't the reason, and it isn't a formal rubric requirement.

mcqs.question: A submission has clean, well-organized code but no setup instructions and an undocumented required environment variable. What's the most likely outcome?
options: The evaluator infers the missing variable from context and scores the code fairly
Some evaluators fail to run it at all and end up scoring only what they can see, effectively nothing
The clean code quality compensates fully for the missing setup steps
Most evaluators will email asking for the missing steps before scoring
mcqs.explanation: A 20-minute skim doesn't leave room to reverse-engineer a broken setup — if the reviewer can't run it, they can't observe most of what was built, and code quality can't compensate for something never seen. Follow-up emails happen sometimes but aren't something to plan around.
